speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Co-operative societies, also known as "co-ops", are membership-based business entities that operate on the principles of self-help and mutual assistance to achieve common economic and social objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: There are also 61 non-credit co-ops spanning various sectors, including retail and social services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This includes the large-scale NTUC co-ops, which serve the general public, and moderate the cost of essential goods and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: There are also other smaller co-ops which serve specific communities, ranging from different professions to ethnic or religious communities and even schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: We also introduced a risk-focused supervisory framework to accord more regulatory oversight of credit co-ops due to their deposit-taking function.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Following the amendments, we implemented prudential requirements on credit co-ops, which included requirements on minimum liquidity and capital, as well as loan restrictions and investment limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Credit co-ops in general have since made good progress in meeting these requirements and improving their financial prudence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Social enterprises are also adopting the co-op model as they consider it to be an effective means to bring together like-minded individuals to address social needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: For example, the Runninghour Co-op, which promotes well-being and integration of persons with special needs through sports, as well as the Silver Caregivers Co-op, which aims to improve the quality of life of caregivers and to build their capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: As part of our regular process, my Ministry has conducted policy reviews with the following two key objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: First, protect the members' interests by strengthening co-ops' competency and regulatory oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This is to ensure that risks are better managed, and members' deposits are better protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Second, ensure that our legislation continues to support the operation and development of co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: We are adopting three strategies to meet the two key objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: First, to strengthen the competency and governance standards of the people running co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Second, to enhance regulatory powers to enable swift intervention in distressed or errant co-ops, so as to better protect co-op members' interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Third, to facilitate co-op operations, by updating or clarifying regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Allow me to elaborate on the first strategy, which is to uplift the competency and governance standards of co-op officers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Notwithstanding that many of the key officers in co-ops are volunteers, it is necessary that they possess the requisite competencies to manage their co-ops in a prudent and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: They are also required to implement adequate risk management policies and internal controls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: To ensure that suitably qualified individuals oversee co-ops, the Bill allows the Minister to make Rules to prescribe mandatory qualification and training requirements for the Committee of Management members and key employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The primary focus at this juncture is on credit co-ops, given that they receive members' deposits and disburse loans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Registry of Co-operative Societies has designed a training programme to ensure that key officers are equipped with the necessary knowledge to discharge their duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Except with the Registrar's approval, an individual who fails to complete such training will be ineligible to be re-elected or co-opted into the Committee of Management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Through subsidiary legislation, we will also issue minimum competency standards on some specified roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The requirements take into consideration both work experience and academic qualifications, and will be tiered according to the size of the credit co-op.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: They will be categorised as either small, medium or large, depending on their total assets and membership size.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: While the new requirements will kick in immediately upon effective date of the Rules for new hires, existing officers who are unable to meet the requirements will be given a transition period to undergo training and upgrade their skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Registry will guide and assist the credit co-ops in this journey of transformation and progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Furthermore, they can only co-opt individuals from their membership base.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Some co-ops have given feedback that they are unable to find suitable individuals with the required competencies from among their members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Hence, to further enable co-ops to strengthen their Committee of Management, the Bill will allow co-ops to appoint up to two individuals into the Committee of Management even if there is no vacancy, and up to the next AGM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: These individuals need not be members of the co-op.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This will facilitate the induction of individuals with relevant skills and knowledge to strengthen the Committee of Management capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: If a co-op is unable to find suitable candidates to fill the Committee of Management positions, especially to meet the required competencies, or should the Registrar deem necessary, the Bill also empowers the Registrar to appoint up to two individuals into the Committee of Management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: These are intended primarily to facilitate swift intervention in weak, distressed or errant co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Allow me to highlight the key amendments in this section.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The first relates to credit co-ops which fail to meet prudential requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: If the credit co-op still fails to rectify its situation, the Registrar may, as a last resort, cancel its registration as a credit co-op.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: These may be necessary to discharge the Registrar's duties under the Act, to investigate possible mismanagement, or on application of a co-op's creditor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill updates the Registrar's powers in these areas to ensure necessary access to the co-op's premises, documents, as well as individuals with the relevant information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Further to this, offence provisions in the Act have also been broadened to include new offences, such as the provision of false and misleading information to the Registrar, obstructing the Registrar's duties or wilful falsification of records.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill ensures that the Registrar is equipped with the necessary powers to take adequate and swift intervention in such scenarios.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Beyond current powers to suspend the activities of a co-op and remove one or more Committee of Management members, the Bill broadens the Registrar's powers to, among other things, suspend a co-op officer for a period not exceeding 24 months, appoint a statutory adviser to advise the Committee of Management or order the co-op to take such remedial action or refrain from doing any act, should there be a misconduct or mismanagement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill also specifies that an individual who has been removed or suspended by the Registrar shall not be eligible to be a Committee of Management member of any co-op or a key employee of a credit co-op, except with the Registrar's approval.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The powers described in this section will only be used as a last resort to protect the co-op or its members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: In the case of a credit co-op, for example, the Registrar's intervention may be necessary to maintain members' confidence, stabilise the co-op and prevent a run on deposits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: In addition, these powers will be exercised after due process and with a channel of appeal to the Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: After all means to save a co-op have been exhausted, it may prove necessary to wind up the co-op if members' interests are at significant risk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Currently, the Registrar may issue a winding up order after an inquiry or examination and when the Registrar is of the opinion that a co-op ought to be wound up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Act also empowers the Registrar to wind up a co-op should it fail to meet basic requirements, such as the minimum number of members or repeatedly failing to conduct an annual general meeting or submit audited financial statements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill broadens the circumstances in which the Registrar can wind up a co-op, to include insolvency, inability to meet financial obligations or if it is no longer in the interest of its members for the co-op to continue its operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: While we strengthen governance standards and enhance regulatory powers, we have also reviewed our legislation to ensure that it supports and facilitates the operations and development of co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: At the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), we see the inherent value of the co-operative model in building social capital and nurturing a more caring and resilient Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Hence, we have reviewed the registration process and eligibility of membership in co-ops to make them more facilitative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: For example, we have lowered the number of individuals required to form a co-op.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This would make it easier for Singaporeans to form co-ops and achieve social objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: There are also existing prohibitions on persons with disabilities, bankrupts or ex-offenders, from being members of co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill removes these outdated prohibitions to ensure a more inclusive co-op movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: We are also reducing the minimum age to become a Committee of Management member, from 21 to 18 years of age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This will especially help to facilitate the participation of tertiary students in joining a Committee of Management of co-ops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: On the issue of capital, members' shares in co-ops are redeemable in nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This would enable co-ops to further build their capital base or meet any applicable capital requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This class of shares may only be issued to Institutional Members, who are better placed to permanently lock in their funds as compared to individual members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Permanent Shares may, however, be transferred to other Institutional Members or bought back by the issuing co-op.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: To provide co-ops with more clarity on the keeping of records and documents, the Bill introduces a five-year retention period and specifies the types of documents that must be retained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Hence, as owners of co-ops, members are expected to play an active role at the AGM and to hold their elected officials accountable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: The Bill also introduces other amendments to make technical edits or to update or clarify administrative processes and timelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: These include, for example, the period by which a co-op shall inform the Registrar and its creditors of a change in its address or in its officers' particulars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: They have contributed in many ways, big and small, to a stronger social fabric by meeting different social and economic needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: This Bill today reflects our balanced approach towards the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: On the other hand, we acknowledge that there is room for co-ops to grow in the social services sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Co-ops are an effective ground-up structure for individuals to form a business to address needs in society or to champion causes they support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
text: Further to our proposed amendments in this Bill, we will continue to review our administrative processes to help facilitate the operations and development of co-ops.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Specifically, I am the CEO of NTUC Fairprice Co-operative and was previously the Chairman of the Singapore National Co-operative Federation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Co-operatives make substantial contributions to our social goals, especially when the economic environments get challenging.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We take our bearing from our social mission to benefit the members, communities and the societies that we operate in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 2012, the United Nations General Assembly declared that year, 2012, as the International Year of Cooperatives, highlighting the important role of co-operatives to socioeconomic development, particularly their impact on poverty reduction, employment generation and social integration.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many of my colleagues had participated and contributed actively at the public consultation period in the first half of 2017.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Registry of Co-operative Societies (RCS) has taken into consideration most of the feedback given and incorporated these in the Co-operative Societies (Amendment) Bill that is being debated in Parliament today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, I would like to raise some remaining concerns.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, on the Registrar's enhanced powers, and these are in sections 9A, 16BB, 59A, 83, 94 and 94A.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Taken together, I recognise that the intention of the Ministry is to better protect members' interests when the Committee of Management is not performing its duties properly or when there has been misconduct and mismanagement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, I fear this intention may lead us to over-regulate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Section 9A itself allows the Registrar to modify the terms and conditions of registration.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, technically, the Registrar will be given wide-ranging powers to wind up any co-op by modifying their terms and conditions of registration.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Section 59A also empowers the Registrar to appoint up to two individuals to serve in the co-op's Committee of Management.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I assume such appointments will only be done in exceptional cases and in consultation with the co-op concerned, whose consent should not be unreasonably withheld.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am raising this point to ensure that the independence of co-ops is not compromised when such powers are conferred to the Registrar.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It would be a sad situation if a co-op is wound up against the wishes of its members.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In section 59(6), the term "manager" has been replaced by "chief executive officer" (CEO).

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The duties of the secretary or treasurer should not be delegated only to the CEO.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, this could also be delegated to the chief financial officer (CFO) or the board secretary or the equivalent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The proposed flexibility in the delegation of duties is to reduce the administrative load on the CEO.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In section 57(3), there is no proposed change on voting mechanism in the case of election or removal of officers that is by secret ballot.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, I propose that this will be aligned to the Companies Act, which allows voting by show of hands.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Although I know it is possible for co-ops to seek exemption from the Registrar for a certain period of time as is currently practised, I think this is administratively cumbersome to monitor and keep track.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In section 72(1) on distribution of net surplus, I note that there are no changes proposed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I believe that, currently, co-ops may only declare and pay dividends, patronage refund and honoraria, collectively referred to as distributions, only from the net surplus, if any, of the preceding financial year.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I say this because this is consistent with the object of promoting the economic interest of its members and it is also consistent with the Companies Act requirement.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the case of the NTUC group of co-operatives, they had historically been conservative in its dividend distributions, resulting in accumulation of net surpluses from past years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As is, 10% of share capital is the maximum allowable under the Co-operative Societies Act to be declared as dividends.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Under the current legislation, the co-op would not be able to declare a dividend even though their financials remain sound.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: By way of comparison, section 403 of the Companies Act states that " o dividend shall be payable to shareholders of any companies except out of profits".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The definition of "profits" in the current practice for companies include accumulated surpluses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications and proposed change, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the purposes of this speech, I shall confine myself with regards to credit co-ops.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Meeting economic and social objectives were the causes for the setting up of these co-operatives in the past but their relevance are being challenged and many new co-operatives and new causes are being explored.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, for the same Thrift and Loan Society, the first wake-up call for them was actually sounded back in 2003, but the amount that was misused at that time was only $40,000 and perhaps did not register on the radar.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clearly, this is a case of once bitten, twice still not very shy!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, it is never too late to reset the button and to prevent such financial mismanagement at any co-operatives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These assets in question are large, and one misstep could have the funds could get wiped off.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question I would like to ask is how are we certain that the people who are currently running our credit co-operatives qualified or trained financially?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If they are not, what further follow-up action will be required, other than instituting qualifications and training requirements?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the records of the co-ops be audited to ensure that their assets were managed competently by qualified officials?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In view of the large amount of funds and assets in the care of co-operatives, besides categorising them according into small, medium and large co-ops, will there be the possibility of introducing ratings for them?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, for the rest of the smaller co-operatives, they would definitely be under the same strain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Where else, besides chit funds, could you squirrel away a small amount of money monthly and get to enjoy loans, bursaries and even, back then, buy household items in instalments?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Co-ops used to provide ease of mind to its members, who were assured that their hard-earned money was slowly growing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Further, to prevent conflict of interest in the running of co-operatives, I would further like to suggest that there be no duplication in the composition of the Committee of Management membership in credit co-ops and that persons related to the Committee of Management be barred from holding management positions in the respective co-operatives as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By doing so, we can prevent the diktat of a particular Committee of Management member prevailing over other co-operatives that he or she may be involved in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications I seek, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It has been 10 years since the Co-operative Societies Act was last amended, and it is timely that the Ministry reviews the laws governing the co-ops and take a harder stance against individuals who seek to exploit co-ops for their own gains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to ensure that such fraud cases are snuffed out and I support the provisions in the Bill, which will provide the Registrar with enhanced regulatory powers to protect the interests of co-op members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what happens if a co-op faces distress not due to fraud, but as a result of its members' negligence?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will ensure that they have the necessary proficiency to handle members' money with sufficient care and reduce the risk of co-ops facing distress due to negligence or a lack of proper training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As it would fit with the Bill's intent to increase competencies of key committee members and the overall corporate governance structure of co-ops, yearly training under the structured proficiency framework should also be made mandatory for key officeholders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that the Senior Minister of State had earlier explained that this was to facilitate the participation of tertiary students.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what is the current proportion of members in the co-ops' committees of management who are aged 25 years old and below?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will a younger person with lesser experience have the right aptitude and the proper knowledge to adequately manage the co-ops' and large amounts of members' money?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps, this can be based on the annual reports which credit co-ops have to submit on an annual basis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Grading the co-ops based on timeliness and completeness of the annual reports as well as on audits conducted by the Ministry would certainly be in the interest of their members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am certain that this would also motivate the credit co-ops' executives and managers to be more accountable to their members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Still on the matter of credit co-ops, I would like to ask if they are still viable and sustainable in this day and age.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Credit co-ops were first introduced in Singapore in the mid-1920s, at a time when moneylending was booming.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There were no financial institutions or banks for wage earners back then who were unable to find financial relief in their times of need and were struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore is now a regional financial hub with world class financial institutions and different moneylending options are readily available.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are Singapore's credit co-op membership trends similar to the membership statistics recorded by the World Council of Credit Unions?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If credit co-ops are indeed losing their relevance, I would urge the Ministry to review the viability and sustainability of credit co-ops in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, the future state of co-ops in Singapore could be social co-ops, those which focus on providing social services for specific groups within our population, such as the disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have some good examples of social co-ops locally, such as the Runninghour Co-operative Ltd, which was cited by the Senior Minister of State earlier.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Italy, where there are various forms of social co-ops, innovative methods have been used to tackle existing societal needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One example is Fuori di Zucca, a social farm which helps to rehabilitate individuals with mental health issues by providing them with a safe working environment on a farm in order to reintegrate them back into society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Belgium, there is a co-operative of freelancer artist who shares better working conditions and also provide access to workplace protection as a group.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, are there any plans by the Ministry to encourage the growth of such social co-ops in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These workers were earning a wage so low that they could barely afford basic necessities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Out of desperation, they chanced upon the idea of operating a co-op by pooling their money together and they opened their own shop to sell necessities at affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The birth of co-ops as business entities thus benefited their members by offering members a higher standard of living through the provision of reliable goods and services, savings during purchases and modest returns from the running of the business.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, co-ops operate mainly in four primary sectors – campus, credit, NTUC, and services.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These co-operatives are governed by their strong social mission to provide a wide range of goods and services to benefit their members and the community at large.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The NTUC sector, one of the oldest and largest co-op sector in Singapore, has the added mission of moderating the cost of living in Singapore to ensure that everyone has access to basic needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Altogether, these 85 co-ops in Singapore have served the specific needs of their members and the community at large.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But compared to other co-ops that are in the business of providing general goods and services, credit co-operatives operate like a quasi-financial institution by providing basic banking services like subscription and deposit savings, fixed savings and loans to their members.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Credit co-ops, like the Singapore Government Staff Credit Co-op Society that was formed in 1925, probably served a purpose historically when the capital and financial market was less mature.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, given today's context where Singapore has a robust and sophisticated banking and finance sector, like my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Melvin Yong, one cannot help but to question the long-term viability of credit co-ops, as well as whether the management committee of these co-ops possess the right skillsets to navigate the increasingly complex operating environment of financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the significant amount of deposits and loans that credit co-ops are dealing with, I welcome the amendment of the Co-operative Societies Bill where the Government, through the Registrar of Co-Operative Societies, is looking at how we can strengthen the governance structure of these co-ops.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compared to banks that operate under stringent regulations by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), credit co-ops appear to be loosely regulated.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the current moment, credit co-ops are regulated by guidelines suggested by the Registrar of Co-operative Societies and their accounts are audited by qualified auditors.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these are first-line measures to safeguard members' interest and to ensure that their savings are secure, these measures may not be sufficient to guarantee that good corporate governance practices are in place.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additional training, and even certification, will help strengthen the competencies of officers who are running co-ops.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the clause sets out the broad rubrics, the devil is always in the details.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Minster clarify how the rules are derived, what these rules would be and how they would be enforced?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that this is a drastic step that is akin to the board of directors stipulating the replacement of the management team in a listed company, can the Minister clarify the guidelines or criteria that would be used by the Registrar to ascertain mismanagement or misconduct?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, what is the profile of the candidates that the Registrar would consider when deciding on who to appoint in the new team?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would they be drawn from the private, non-governmental organisations or the public sector?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the event when such an action is taken, how will the Government manage the communications such that members of the co-op and the public would not perceive that the Government is taking over the running of the co-op?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I have spoken about the need to regulate the governance of credit co-ops, it is also important for the Government to facilitate growth and development as they allow people to get together based on common interests and for the common goal of furthering the welfare of the society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentioned by the Senior Minister of State earlier, the Runninghour co-op is an inclusive running club that integrates people with special needs through running.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Silver Caregivers Co-op aims to be a one-stop centre to better the quality of life for caregivers of elderly and the Silver Horizon Travel Co-op is a social enterprise that promotes active living and learning for elderly by using travel as a platform.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are some examples of how co-ops in Singapore have successfully served a specific purpose for a larger good.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Deputy Speaker, I conclude my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There has been a steady increase in the number of co-operatives in Singapore serving a variety of needs, a strong recognition of the effectiveness of the cooperative business model.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is heartening to see members of the public coming together to support each other in a spirit of self-help and mutual assistance, and the Government must do all it can to support this ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Bill's bid to enact tougher rules to ensure co-operatives, the members and their funds are not abused for personal benefits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As an entity addressing social needs, co-ops are well-placed to lead the way in demonstrating how doing good can also mean doing well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I refer to the new section 32C, which requires credit societies to inform the Registrar of any new developments or changed circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Bill does not specify any penalties for failing to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To ensure credit societies comply with these new rules, should we not also impose punitive measures?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, I would like to raise a point about the new section 9A, which allows the Registrar to modify the terms and conditions of the registration of a society at any time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, the new section 16BB empowers the Registrar to modify terms and conditions for a non-credit society to become a credit society and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Registrar must notify the society in writing informing them about the changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But in line with the spirit of the Bill to increase transparency, could we also disclose this information to members of the co-op and even members of the public?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Greater transparency on how co-ops are governed would be in line with the general objectives of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I refer to clause 44 which empowers the Registrar or an authorised person to inspect documents and information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As with many of the recent Bills, we are providing extended powers usually reserved for the Police, for example, to enter and search premises without warrant, take "any relevant things" and retain it for as long as is deemed necessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 63 also makes it an offence for individuals who delay or obstruct the discharge of the Registrar's duties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such deposits should not be treated differently from deposits in our banks or other registered financial entities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, with reference to the amendment to allow a co-op or the Registrar to co-opt up to two new members to the committee of management, even if there is no vacancy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the objective is to facilitate the introduction of competent persons to strengthen the committee, which will require talents with relevant experience in finance, accounting, credit, risk management and compliance, a co-op should be able to include more members if necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the matter has been dealt with in Court, the fact that the two employees were able to carry on with the deceit for so many years underscored the need to regulate co-operatives more stringently and ensure that proper governance procedures are in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can give greater confidence to members, assure them that their savings are protected and continue to uphold public confidence in co-operatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One key area that needs to be tackled is in the appointment of credible and qualified individuals into the management committees of co-ops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I support the proposed changes on this matter as they will go a long way in professionalising the co-ops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also support the enhanced regulatory powers that the Registry will have, for instance, in taking action when the management committee is not performing its duty, as well as in requiring co-ops to inform the Registry on developments that might adversely affect members' interests or its ability to meet financial obligations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If so, how many co-ops were in this position and have steps been taken to rectify the problems?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There could be also members of credit co-ops who have taken on loans and have defaulted on them, especially where the payment is not made through salary check-offs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To ensure that co-operatives have competent management and staff members, professional training and upgrading of skills is required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As there are many types of courses, will the Registry identify relevant training areas for key committee and staff members?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, while these measures are necessary to improve the governance standards of co-operatives, it will also involve administrative processes that will take time and incur costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must be able to strike a good balance between the robustness of governance and the ease of operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Also, what is the timeframe given to co-ops to get all their processes in place?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some co-ops, like the Singapore Government Staff Credit Co-op, have adopted a whistleblower policy and the terms are clearly spelt out on its website.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do encourage the Registry to consider that this is something that all co-ops should perhaps adopt.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Credit terms should similarly be made available to members and the public on their website.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will further promote accountability, responsibility and transparency in the management of co-ops and protect whistleblowers who alert the authorities about lapses or other matters of concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The measures proposed in this Bill would not eliminate fraud or lapses completely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It would not be reasonable to expect that it will do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But they will go a long way in ensuring that the system is transparent and robust without sacrificing on ease of operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Allow me to address the points they have raised in three broad categories.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, regulatory powers of the Registrar; second, issues relating to credit co-ops; and third, facilitation and development of the co-op sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Darryl David, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Melvin Yong all supported strengthening the Registrar's powers to protect the interests of the co-ops' members.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Gan and Mr Yam even suggested further enhancement to the powers due to the concerns raised in their respective speeches.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng highlighted some provisions in relation to the Registrar's enhanced powers and raised concerns over possible over-regulation.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Before addressing these specific concerns, I would like to share our guiding principles.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As a fundamental principle, my Ministry upholds the fact that co-ops are owned by members who have common bonds.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We recognise that members may have strong attachment to their own co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They choose their own leaders to manage the affairs of the co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, the Registrar's duty is not to take over the responsibilities of the co-ops' members and Committees of Management.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Registrar's duty is to regulate so as to protect the members' interests and the co-op movement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We need to ensure members' deposits and interests are protected.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Credit co-ops are already subjected to governance and prudential requirements.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The majority of them are complying with or are making good progress in meeting these requirements.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, there are still gaps when it comes to dealing with situations of mismanagement, misconduct, distress and crisis.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, instead of imposing more stringent control requirements on all credit co-ops, we have decided to strengthen the Registrar's ability to protect the members' interests in such extreme situations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Registrar's powers in section 94 and 94A, for example, are meant to protect members' interests and the co-op movement by maintaining stability, rectifying weaknesses and strengthening organisational competencies in severe circumstances or after an inquiry.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Thirdly, the Registrar will intervene and act to protect only as a last resort, in other words, in situations of distress or mismanagement, as described earlier.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Lastly, to ensure a check and balance, due process and an appeal channel are provided for in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Now, let me go into the specific concerns raised by the Members on the enhancement of the Registrar's powers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah raised a specific concern that the Registrar may modify the terms and conditions of a co-op's registration and subsequently wind up the co-op should it fail to meet them.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We proposed this amendment to cater for possible situations, such as a co-op changing its social mission or business activities, which may render the terms and conditions of its registration no longer relevant.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, there is the need to make the modification.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Any decision to wind up a co-op on account of failure to meet a registration condition would only be in an extreme case where significant risks to its members or society have been identified, and also after due process.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether, in the spirit of increasing transparency, the Registry could disclose the modified terms and conditions to the members and even the public.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, given that co-ops are membership-based organisations, there is no necessity to disclose such information to the general public.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Two Members have also highlighted the amendment in which the Registrar may appoint up to two individuals to serve in the Committee of Management of a co-op.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As Committee of Managements of credit co-ops should possess requisite competencies to oversee the co-ops effectively, Mr Gan suggested that a co-op or the Registrar should be allowed to appoint more than two new members.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As co-ops are essentially membership-based organisations, we recognise that the leadership must have the support of the members through open and fair elections of officers during the general meetings.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah is correct in his assumption that this would only be done in exceptional cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If the Committee of Management lacks certain capabilities, the co-op should find competent persons to serve on the Committee of Managment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In fact, we allow the co-op to appoint up to two members to serve on the Committee of Management.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If they are unable to find such persons on their own, the Registrar may appoint up to two individuals to serve in the Committee of Management to ensure compliance with the requirements or proper management of the co-op.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Darryl David asked what guidelines or criteria would be applied before the Registrar acts to remove a Committee of Management, and appoint one or more individuals to take over the management and administration of a co-op.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such a protective measure would likely only be undertaken after an inquiry has been conducted or there is evidence demonstrating that the actions of the Committee of Management has put the co-op in a vulnerable or risky state or that there has been mismanagement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We hope that should such a need arise, there are respected individuals from within the sector who would step up to take on such a role.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are first and foremost looking for individuals with integrity and the necessary competencies and knowledge of the sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We would also seek inputs from our stakeholders including the industry body, the Singapore National Co-operative Federation (SNCF) and the Central Co-operative Fund (CCF) Committee.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The involvement of the Registrar in this regard aims to stabilise the co-op and maintain members' confidence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We believe it would provide assurance to members, especially in times of distress or crisis.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Louis Ng raised a concern on whether extended powers are necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I have earlier mentioned that we are concerned about situations of mismanagement, misconduct, distress and crisis.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence we have decided to strengthen the Registrar's ability to protect the members' interests in such circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: One of which is to ensure that the Registrar can properly investigate into matters which led to or caused these situations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Registrar would exercise the power of search and seize if there is reason to suspect that an offence under the Act has been committed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In addition, the Registrar must have reasonable cause to believe the document or item is necessary for the purpose of obtaining evidence of the offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This power is especially critical to enable the Registrar to uncover the truth and act swiftly, particularly for credit co-ops where a crisis situation could cause a run in the co-op, and adversely affect the sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I will now move on to the next set of comments and queries on credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the relevance of credit co-ops in this day and age.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: My Ministry believes that there is still a place for credit co-ops in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Notwithstanding that the membership base of credit co-ops is fairly small and has remained relatively stable in the last few years, credit co-ops still play an important social role in serving their members, especially so in promoting savings and giving loans at affordable interest rates to members in need.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As co-ops are less profit driven compared to financial institutions, they are more willing to go the extra mile for their members by extending loans to the lower-income earners and rescheduling members' loans to help them tide over difficult periods.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Given the self-help element and social objectives, co-ops are regulated by the Registry of Co-operative Societies under MCCY.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Many credit co-ops' members are Singaporeans who can ill-afford to lose their savings in the credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, it is necessary to ensure that their deposits are prudently managed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As leaders of credit co-ops, the Committee of Management members and key employees have a responsibility to act prudently and be accountable to the members.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In order to properly discharge their duties, Committee of Management members and key employees have to be competent and undergo relevant training.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In expressing support for raising the governance of credit co-ops to better protect members' deposits, Mr Darryl David, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Desmond Choo have asked for more information on the training and qualification requirements that will be introduced for the Committee of Management members and key employees of credit co-ops and how these will be enforced.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Additionally, Mr Choo asked about the assistance provided to the co-ops in view of the possible additional administrative costs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Registry has worked with SNCF to develop a customised training programme for all Committee of Management members of credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The training programme covers topics such as governance, internal controls, regulatory requirements and best practices.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This training is heavily subsidised by the CCF.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As credit co-ops vary in size, we have applied a tiered approach in implementing the requirements.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While we raise the bar, we also ensure that support is provided to the sector to assist them in meeting these new standards.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether there are other action plans besides instituting qualifications and training requirements for the key officers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have, in fact, updated the Code of Governance in 2016 and provided a self-evaluation checklist which credit co-ops will be required to submit to the Registry.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In 2017, the Registry and SNCF further developed specific guidelines on internal controls, loans management and investment management, which will be rolled out to the credit co-ops this year to strengthen their capabilities and processes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, we will work hand-in-hand with SNCF and all the credit co-ops' key officers to support them on this journey of upskilling.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yam suggested that persons related to the Committee of Management be barred from holding management positions in their co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We would like to share that while some Committee of Management members may be involved in the operations of their co-op, the Act requires the majority of a credit co-op's Committee of Management to be independent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A credit co-op's audit committee shall also comprise at least three members who shall be independent of the co-op.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Additionally, all Committee of Management members must disclose any conflict of interest.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the Code of Governance, it is stated that a credit co-op should have policies to manage conflict of interest, for example, a Committee of Management member with conflict of interest should be excluded from the relevant discussions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Code also states that the roles of the Committee of Management and key staff officers should be clearly defined.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In addition, the Chairman and the CEO should be separate persons to ensure an appropriate balance of power, increased accountability and greater capacity of the Committee of Management for independent decision making.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: On Mr Yam's suggestion for no duplication of Committee of Management in co-ops, we are conscious that such a requirement would have trade-offs and implications for the sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Notwithstanding, we will consider the matter and discuss with our stakeholders in our next review of the Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Gan suggested that deposits in credit co-ops should be covered by deposit insurance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We would like to assure Mr Gan that while there is no DIS for the credit co-ops, we have put in place various prudential and governance requirements to instil financial prudence and manage the risks of credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yam asked if the records of co-ops will be audited.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In addition, they will undergo special audits conducted by the Registry.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Desmond Choo has asked how much time credit co-ops will be given to ensure that processes are in place.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The special audits are primarily governance and internal controls audits, aimed at helping credit co-ops identify gaps and lapses in their operations and existing processes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Co-ops will be provided recommendations on how to address the findings and strengthen their operations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The co-op's Committee of Management will thereafter propose their management action plan and proposed timeline in the audit report, which the Registry will monitor.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Choo also asked about the bad debts of credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In writing off the loans, credit co-ops follow the Financial Reporting Standards and their own internal policies.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Alex Yam asked about introducing ranking or rating systems on the credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As membership-based entities, there is no public ranking or rating of the credit co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members should be aware of their co-ops' information through the co-ops' websites, annual reports and audited financial statements, which are tabled at the AGMs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members can raise questions regarding co-ops' matters during these meetings.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If there are adverse findings on any co-ops, appropriate information will be shared with members by the Registrar.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested including punitive measures should a credit co-op not comply with the requirement to provide information under section 32C.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We would like to clarify that this would be captured under section 100 of the Co-operative Societies Act, whereby it is an offence if a co-op neglects or refuses to do any act as required.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Lastly, I greatly appreciate my colleagues' recognition of our efforts to facilitate the operations of co-ops and support us on our amendments to further develop the co-op movement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We agree with Mr Melvin Yong that there is potential for growth for co-ops in the social services and we hope to see them playing a bigger role in the community.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Through this Bill, we have introduced some key changes to further develop the sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These include, for example, reducing the minimum number of individuals required to form a co-op as well as reducing the age limit for Committee of Management members, which will help bring in more youth leaders into the movement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will continue to review our regulatory and administrative requirements to ensure they are facilitative for the setting up and operations of co-operatives.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also continue to work closely with our stakeholders, SNCF and the CCF Committee, to further develop the sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: SNCF as the industry body of co-ops, is funded by the CCF and has various programmes to build awareness and promote the co-op movement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These include roadshows, educational talks in schools, cooperative-related competitions, scholarships and other outreach programmes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The CCF also provides grants to assist eligible new co-ops with their start-up costs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For existing co-ops, there are CCF grants and schemes to develop their capacities and capabilities to help them develop and grow.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They include grants for the training of cooperative officers, purchase of IT systems, upgrading of office premises, audit fees, marketing and accounting services.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I would now like to address some specific queries regarding the amendments to facilitate and develop the co-op sector.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As an effort to rejuvenate the co-op movement, the industry body has been ramping up its youth outreach to raise awareness of the co-op model of enterprise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Even though younger members may lack business and management experience, I believe they can contribute in other ways at the board level, by developing strategies on the use of social media to reach out to new markets, for example, extending new services to members or to understudy experienced and competent leaders as part of succession planning.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: On the replacement of the term "manager" with "chief executive officer", we would like to clarify that there has been no change in policy.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah can be assured that the CEO may be assisted by his staff or agents as appropriate, such as the CFO.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: But the CEO will retain the overall responsibility for the proper running of the co-op.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah also proposed for the voting of election or removal of officers by a show of hands instead of secret ballot.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A co-op is different from companies as the members know each other through common bond or interest.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Being in the same community or organisation, some may fear possible negative repercussions should their votes be known to other members.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We understand that a secret ballot may not be necessary for co-ops with mainly institutional members, for example, and hence, has been amenable to granting exemptions upon request.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Seah also noted that under cooperative legislation, co-ops may only pay dividends from the current year's surplus.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He has asked for this Bill to allow co-ops to draw down on past reserves.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Given its social mission, a co-op should be prudent, especially when it has made a loss.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It should not incur additional expenditure by declaring dividends and eating into its reserves.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We acknowledge Mr Seah's argument that notwithstanding a co-op has made a loss in a financial year, it could, in fact, have positive or healthy accumulated reserves.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The definition of what constitutes as healthy reserves, however, may be subjective.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Desmond Choo inquired on whistleblowing policies for co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the Code of Governance, the Committee of Managements are advised to implement a whistleblowing policy for staff, and any other person, to raise concerns about possible improprieties in confidence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While we strengthen our regulatory oversight of credit co-ops, we are mindful not to burden the sector with additional compliance costs, where possible.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We put forth the competency framework for the key credit co-ops' officers and enhanced the Registrar's abilities to act and protect the members' interests in severe circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is especially pertinent in the case of credit co-ops, where panic among members could cause a run on deposits, for example.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: At the same time, co-ops are still relevant and they are an important form of social enterprise, which contribute to our nation's social and economic fabric.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Hence, our legislation makes it easier to set up and operate co-ops.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We hope to see more and better co-ops in various sectors, such as social service, silver and youth, thus making a positive difference to the lives of fellow Singaporeans.
